subject: mathematics
question_text: If A is the matrix with rows (3, −4) and (1, −1), then show that for every integer n ≥ 1, Aⁿ is the matrix with rows (1+2n, −4n) and (n, 1−2n).

mark_split.label: Multiply Aᵏ by A and simplify each entry
Conclude by the principle of induction

verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, FAST TRACK IPE for Jr. Students — Mathematics-IA (2026-27 edition), book p.42, chapter 5 MATRICES, Short Answer question 10(i). Only the question was taken. The solution, the step order and the mark split are this answer book's own work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S: the Mathematics-IA volume prints no per-step mark allocation on any answer. The 1+2+1 shape puts half the marks on the inductive multiplication, because that is the only step where the arithmetic can go wrong and the only step that actually proves anything; the base case and the closing appeal to the principle of induction are each short but each is a whole mark, since an answer missing either is not a proof. Independently checked before authoring: the claimed form was multiplied out at n = 1, 2 and 3 and gave rows (3, −4)/(1, −1), (5, −8)/(2, −3) and (7, −12)/(3, −5), which match the formula exactly. Paper position: Maths-1A Section B prints eight short answers of which the student writes any six, each worth 4 marks, under the 2026-27 pattern; Matrices supplies one of them. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

recall_prompt: Say how you would prove this — say what you check first, what you assume, what you multiply, and how you finish.

steps.label: Check n = 1
steps.margin_note: First mark. Put n = 1 into the claimed form and compare it with A itself: 1 + 2(1) = 3 and 1 − 2(1) = −1, so the two matrices are the same.
steps.memory_tip: Base case first: put n = 1 into the claimed form and compare it with A itself.
lines: Let P(n) be the given statement about Aⁿ.
Putting n = 1 in the given form:
Both agree, so P(1) is true.

recall.must_convey: That n = 1 is substituted into the claimed form and the result is compared with A itself, and the two match.
accept: put n equals one in the given formula and check it against A itself
for n equals one the formula gives three minus four one minus one which is A
verify the base case by substituting n equals one
n equals one pettina formula A ne istundi, so base case correct
start by testing the statement at n equals one

steps.why: Induction needs a first true case to stand on. Without P(1) the chain of implications has nothing to start from and proves nothing.
common_mistakes: Skipping n = 1 and starting straight from the assumption.
Writing the n = 1 matrix without comparing it with A.

steps.label: Assume for n = k
steps.margin_note: No mark of its own, but the next step is meaningless without it. Write the assumed matrix out in full — the inductive step multiplies this exact matrix by A.
steps.memory_tip: Write the assumed matrix out in full, because the next step multiplies that exact matrix by A.
lines: Assume P(k) is true for some integer k ≥ 1:

recall.must_convey: That the result is ASSUMED true for some integer n = k, with the assumed matrix written out.
accept: assume the result holds for n equals k and write that matrix out
suppose A to the power k has rows one plus two k minus four k and k one minus two k
take the statement as true for some k and use it
n equals k ki result nijam ani anukuntam
let the formula be true for a general k
reject: assume it is true for all n
it is true for k plus one

steps.why: This is an assumption about ONE value k, not about every n. Assuming it for all n would assume the whole result and prove nothing.
common_mistakes: Saying "assume it is true for all n", which assumes what is being proved.
Leaving the assumed matrix unwritten, so the next multiplication has nothing to start from.

steps.label: Multiply Aᵏ by A
steps.margin_note: Half the marks. Use A^(k+1) = Aᵏ·A, not A·Aᵏ from scratch. Then rewrite each entry so that k + 1 is visible: 2k + 3 is 1 + 2(k+1), and −2k − 1 is 1 − 2(k+1).
steps.memory_tip: After multiplying, rewrite every entry so k + 1 shows: 2k + 3 is 1 + 2(k+1).
lines: That is P(k+1). So P(k) ⇒ P(k+1).

recall.must_convey: That A to the power k+1 is written as Aᵏ times A, the product is worked out, and each entry is rewritten so that it is the claimed form with n replaced by k + 1.
accept: write A to the k plus one as A to the k times A and multiply row into column
multiply the assumed matrix by A and rewrite the entries in terms of k plus one
the product gives two k plus three which is one plus two times k plus one
A power k ni A tho multiply cheste k plus one form vasthundi
show that the answer is the same formula with n replaced by k plus one
reject: find A to the k plus one
it is true for k plus one
heard_as: A to the k plus one
A to the k into A

steps.why: The whole proof is this one implication. Getting the product right is only half the work — the entries must then be rearranged so a reader can SEE the claimed form with k + 1 in place of n.
common_mistakes: Stopping at 2k + 3 without showing it equals 1 + 2(k+1).
Dropping a minus sign when multiplying −4k by −1.
Multiplying A by Aᵏ in the wrong order and losing track of the entries.

steps.label: Conclude by induction
steps.margin_note: Last mark. Name the principle of mathematical induction. The two facts proved — P(1) true, and P(k) leading to P(k+1) — are what the principle needs, and saying so is what turns two calculations into a proof.
steps.memory_tip: Two facts earn the conclusion: P(1) is true, and P(k) leads to P(k+1). Name the principle.
lines: P(1) is true, and P(k) ⇒ P(k+1) for every k ≥ 1.
By the principle of mathematical induction, P(n)
is true for every integer n ≥ 1.

recall.must_convey: That both induction conditions have been met and the principle of mathematical induction is named to give the result for every n ≥ 1.
accept: since it is true for one and true for k plus one whenever true for k it holds for all n by induction
by the principle of mathematical induction the formula is true for every integer n greater than or equal to one
both conditions hold so induction gives the result for all n
rendu conditions unnayi kabatti induction valla anni n ki nijam
the principle of induction completes the proof for every n
heard_as: n greater than or equal to one

steps.why: The two earlier steps only cover n = 1 and one implication. The principle of induction is the theorem that turns those two facts into a statement about every n, so it has to be named.
common_mistakes: Writing only "hence proved" without naming the principle of induction.
Claiming the result for all real n; the proof covers integers n ≥ 1 only.
